boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Fort Davidson (Pilot Knob) record (September 27, 1864) in Price's Missouri Expedition [September-October 1864]. The September 26 skirmishes in Arcadia Valley and at Shut-in Gap, Ewing's retreat to Leasburg and Shelby's operations on the railroad are context. Campaign-wide marches, recruiting, destruction, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Garrison and Army of Missouri; the live field reads zero. Price entered Missouri on September 19 with nearly 12,000 men, 8,000 of them armed, and fourteen guns, and reported that information at Fredericktown put the enemy at Ironton at about 1,500; he attacked with Fagan's and Marmaduke's divisions while Shelby's was detached. Britton gives Ewing's force as 489 recently organized infantry plus 562 men of experienced units, 1,051 in all, with about 100 armed citizens and a company of Black men, and says about 5,600 men made the assault.
claims.rationale: An army-wide figure eight days earlier, a pre-battle intelligence estimate and a history's counts; no matched return at the assault. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Britton describes Fort Davidson as an irregular hexagonal work with a ditch ten feet wide and six feet four inches deep, overlooked from Shepherd's Mountain and Pilot Knob, which engineers had judged indefensible against a force with good batteries; Ewing added two rifle-pits and cleared the nearest hillsides. Price says Shepherd's Mountain completely commanded the fortifications and that Marmaduke placed artillery there.
claims.rationale: Ground and works described by a history and an interested report; no map verification. The fort predates Ewing's arrival but he added works, so the phase is left unresolved.

claims.value: NPS and Britton give Saint Louis as the expedition's objective. Britton says Ewing was instructed to hold Pilot Knob if practicable until it was known whether more than Shelby's division was present, and that he resolved to defend it as long as possible to delay the advance. Price says Shelby was sent to cut the railroad so that A. J. Smith could not reinforce the garrison.
claims.rationale: Stated aims from a summary, a history and an interested report.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory. Price says his troops were repulsed and that the enemy evacuated the fort in the night; Britton says the repulse was complete and Price could not rally his men. NPS says the Federals evacuated the fort during the night.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 1,684 total (US 184; CS 1,500); the live field reads 1,800 (US 800; CS 1,000). Britton gives Ewing's report of 200 killed, wounded and missing over the defence of the passes and the retreat to Leasburg, Ewing's estimate of 1,500 Confederate killed and wounded, and Mackey's statement of 1,164 lost in twenty minutes and not less than 1,500 in all; he says Price never reported his casualties. Price gives no figure for Fagan's division and 14 officers and 80 men killed and wounded in Marmaduke's, a figure that follows his account of the pursuit.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

Rosecrans's, Pleasonton's and Curtis's reports, the subordinate Union and Confederate reports in Volume XLI Part 1, the organization of Price's army (No. 89), Maclean's itinerary (No. 90), the Price Court of Inquiry, Hinton's 1865 Rebel Invasion of Missouri and Kansas, maps and returns remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family (the NPS battle page plus the frozen Arnold rows). Wiley Britton's The Civil War on the Border, volume II (Putnam, 1899) is a retrospective history by a Union participant; by its preface the larger operations are based mainly on the published official reports, so it is not independent of the Price report family. Price's September 19 and November 2 dispatches and his December 28, 1864 report (Official Records Series I, Volume XLI, Part 1, No. 88) are one family of interested Confederate accounts. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
